subject: Anthropology
title: Class and Inequality
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Class and Inequality.

hook.text: Caste is fixed. Class is supposed to be flexible. But in practice, class can be just as sticky as caste.

buildup.text: Class systems rank people by wealth, education, and occupation. In theory, movement between classes is possible.

discovery.text: Marx defined class by your relation to production: owners exploit workers. Weber added status and political power.

twist.text: Meritocracy is the promise, but inheritance, networks, and education reproduce class across generations.

climax.text: Class is the engine of modern inequality. It shapes your health, education, lifespan, and opportunities from birth.

punchline.text: Class moves, but it rarely moves far.

quiz.question: How does class differ from caste?
options: Class is theoretically open to mobility while caste is fixed at birth

details.summary: Social class divides societies by economic resources, prestige, and power. Unlike caste, class boundaries are theoretically permeable, but in practice, class position is strongly inherited through family wealth, education, and social networks.
details.whyItMatters: Class is the dominant form of social stratification in industrial and post-industrial societies. Understanding how kinship transmits class advantage reveals why inequality persists across generations despite ideologies of meritocracy.
takeaways: Social class divides societies by wealth, prestige, and power
Class position is strongly inherited through family resources
Meritocracy ideology masks how kinship transmits class advantage

faq.question: How do families transmit class position across generations?
faq.answer: Through inherited wealth, access to quality education, social networks, cultural knowledge, and even accent and manners. Pierre Bourdieu called these advantages social and cultural capital — resources that are passed through families alongside economic wealth.

faq.question: Is social mobility increasing or decreasing globally?
faq.answer: Research shows social mobility has stagnated or decreased in many wealthy nations. Rising housing costs, education costs, and wealth concentration make it harder for each generation to surpass their parents' class position despite widespread belief in meritocracy.
